meta.title: Who really said "Lose As If You Like It, and Win As If You Are Used to It"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Emerson. The sporting adage is anonymous — in print in full by 1929, quoted there as already current, with half of it in print by 1920; first credited to Thomas Hitchcock in 1943.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Lose As If You Like It, and Win As If You Are Used to It'?
meta.ogDescription: Quote Investigator found no evidence Emerson said it. The adage is anonymous — in print in full by 1929, half of it by 1920, and credited to Thomas Hitchcock only from 1943.

answer.label: Not Ralph Waldo Emerson — an anonymous sporting adage
answer.authorDates: A turf-and-polo maxim · in print in full by 1929, quoted as already current; half of it in print by 1920
answer.sourceLine: Quote Investigator traced the saying and found no evidence connecting it to Emerson: the earliest known trace is an unattributed half-line in a 1920 tennis report in The Times of London, and the first full version sits in Harry S. Page’s 1929 racing memoir Between the Flags — printed inside quotation marks as an adage already in circulation, with no author named. A name is attached only from 1943, when a Texas newspaper signed it “Thomas Hitchcock” — and even then the polo star’s son was quoting it as his father’s advice, not his father’s invention.

source.heading: Where the saying actually comes from

docMeta.dd: The Times (London), 27 April 1920 — report on the Tennis Amateur Championship
Between the Flags: The Recollections of a Gentleman Rider
Harry S. Page · The Derrydale Press, New York · 1929, p. 209
Lockhart Post Register, Lockhart, Texas, 22 April 1943 — signed “Thomas Hitchcock”

source.excerpt: In racing, the rough and the smooth are so quickly interchangeable that the only path safe from the ridiculous, is the one guarded by “Win as if you are used to it. Lose as if you liked it.”
trail: 1920 — half the adage, no author. A tennis report in The Times of London praises the player E. L. Phillips for having “learned the most difficult thing in all games, to lose as if he liked it” — the earliest relevant trace, transcribed by Quote Investigator ↗.

1929 — both halves, in quotation marks. Harry S. Page’s racing memoir Between the Flags quotes it as an existing rule of the turf: “Win as if you are used to it. Lose as if you liked it.” No author is named, and none is implied (citation and page reference at QI ↗).

1942–1943 — a name attaches. The Edwardsville Intelligencer in Illinois ran it as unsigned filler in 1942; the following April a Texas paper, the Lockhart Post Register, printed it signed “Thomas Hitchcock.” A year after that Newsweek quoted the polo champion Tommy Hitchcock Jr. ↗ crediting the advice to his father.

Nowhere in Emerson. The line appears in no section of Wikiquote’s Emerson page ↗ — not among the work-by-work sourced quotations, nor in its Attributed, Disputed or Misattributed lists. Emerson died in 1882 ↗, decades before the adage is first documented in print.
source.excerptNote: Page sets the maxim inside quotation marks and names nobody — the standard signal that a writer is passing on a saying already in circulation rather than minting one. This is the earliest full-form appearance Quote Investigator has located.

source.rightsNote: The exact modern wording is an anonymous adage with no identified author, so there is no creator to whom a copyright could attach and no basis for calling this specific phrasing public domain — the status is left open rather than asserted. The two early printings that carry it, the 1920 Times tennis report and Harry S. Page’s Between the Flags (The Derrydale Press, 1929), were both published before 1931 and are themselves in the public domain in the United States, but neither is the origin of the saying.

author.name: Thomas Hitchcock Sr.
author.kicker: The earliest name any source attaches to it
author.heading: The man the adage actually stuck to
author.metaLine: 1860–1941 · American polo pioneer and steeplechase trainer
author.bio: Thomas Hitchcock Sr. organised the first polo match on Long Island in 1877, helped establish the Meadowbrook Polo Club in 1881, and became one of the earliest Americans rated at the maximum ten goals. He is equally remembered as the father of American steeplechasing — he trained thoroughbreds, won the American Grand National with Good and Plenty in 1906, and was elected to the National Museum of Racing and Hall of Fame in 1973. He is the first person any source names in connection with this adage, but the credit reaches us second-hand through his son Tommy Hitchcock Jr., who repeated it as something his father emphasised — and the maxim was already in print years before either Hitchcock was linked to it.

cite.sourceCitation: Earliest documented in Harry S. Page, Between the Flags: The Recollections of a Gentleman Rider (New York: The Derrydale Press, 1929), 209, where the maxim is set in quotation marks as an adage already in circulation, with no author named; a partial precursor appears in an unsigned tennis report in The Times (London), 27 April 1920. Not found in the works of Ralph Waldo Emerson. See Quote Investigator, "Quote Origin: Lose As If You Like It, and Win As If You Are Used to It," 14 September 2012.

misattribution.heading: Who gets the credit, and why none of it holds
misattribution.intro: This is a proverb that has been handed a different owner roughly once a decade. Quote Investigator’s own question opens by listing eight candidate names; its conclusion keeps none of them as the coiner.

items.why: Quote Investigator ↗ reports it has “found no compelling evidence linking the coinage of the saying to Emerson or Golnik.” No essay, lecture, letter or journal entry is ever named, and the aggregator pages that carry the Emerson credit — AZQuotes among them ↗ — give no source line at all. The line is also absent from every section of Wikiquote’s Emerson page ↗, sourced and unsourced alike.

The 1997 Dictionary of Quotations in Communications printed the “lose as if you enjoyed it for a change” variant under Golnik’s name with no citation attached — more than half a century after the adage was already circulating in print, as Quote Investigator documents ↗.

items.tag: Used it, did not coin it
items.why: The strongest of the claims, and still not coinage. His son told Newsweek in 1944 that “Father always emphasized being a good sportsman” and quoted the maxim — but the adage was already in print, unattributed, in full in 1929 and in part in 1920. QI’s verdict ↗ is that there is evidence Hitchcock Sr. used it and that his son relayed it.

items.who: Jock Whitney, Mrs. F. Ambrose Clark, Desi Arnaz, Rosalind Russell
items.why: Each is recorded passing the maxim on between the 1950s and the 1960s — Time crediting the counsel to the late Mrs. F. Ambrose Clark, Whitney attributing it to an old trainer who advised his mother, Arnaz recalling it from a school locker-room sign. Quote Investigator ↗ concludes they “relayed the saying, but did not formulate it.”

misattribution.truthLine: The honest answer is that nobody owns this one. In the earliest citations known to Quote Investigator ↗ the adage is anonymous — a piece of racecourse and polo-field wisdom that was already common property by 1929, and that acquired famous owners only after the fact.

context.heading: Why a locker-room proverb ended up wearing Emerson’s name
lead: This is a working maxim, not a literary one. It grew up in the horse-racing and polo world — the domain where a man might win the American Grand National one week and be picking himself out of the turf the next — and its whole point is behavioural: keep your face the same in both directions. Harry S. Page put it in his 1929 racing memoir as the one guard against looking ridiculous, and by the 1950s it had migrated to a locker-room sign in a Miami high school, where Desi Arnaz read it ↗ and later wrote it down.

Proverbs with no author are unstable, and unstable quotations drift toward famous names. Emerson is one of the strongest attractors in English — aphoristic, endlessly anthologised, and safely out of copyright — so a well-made anonymous line about winning and losing gets filed under his name and then copied from database to database. The tell is what is missing: no essay, no lecture, no journal entry, no page number. Quote sites that credit him ↗ give no source at all, because there is none to give.
detailsBody: 1943 — the Lockhart Post Register in Texas runs it as a freestanding line signed “Thomas Hitchcock.”
1944 — Newsweek’s obituary-adjacent profile “Ten-Goal Hitchcock” quotes Tommy Hitchcock Jr. crediting the advice to his father; Reader’s Digest reprints it from Newsweek in 1946.
1954–1961 — Time attaches it to Mrs. F. Ambrose Clark, Desi Arnaz recalls it from a school locker room in 1955, and Rosalind Russell offers it as advice to a newspaper columnist in 1961.
1997 — the Dictionary of Quotations in Communications assigns it to Eric Mark Golnik with no citation, seeding a second false credit alongside Emerson’s.
context.pull: Page printed it inside quotation marks in 1929 — the mark of a writer passing on a proverb, not coining one.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator found no compelling evidence linking the coinage of the saying to Emerson or Golnik; the earliest relevant citation is a precursor in The Times of London, 27 April 1920, praising E. L. Phillips for learning "the most difficult thing in all games, to lose as if he liked it"; the fuller form appears in Harry S. Page, Between the Flags: The Recollections of a Gentleman Rider (Derrydale Press, New York, 1929), p. 209, in quotation marks and unattributed; the Edwardsville Intelligencer ran it as filler on 3 June 1942; the Lockhart Post Register (Lockhart, Texas), 22 April 1943, signed it "Thomas Hitchcock"; Newsweek's May 1944 "Ten-Goal Hitchcock" quoted Tommy Hitchcock Jr. crediting his father; Reader's Digest reprinted it in 1946 crediting Newsweek; Time (1954) attached it to Mrs. F. Ambrose Clark; Desi Arnaz recalled it from a school locker-room sign in American Magazine (1955); Rosalind Russell repeated it in 1961; Reader's Digest printed the "for a change" variant in 1963; the 1997 Dictionary of Quotations in Communications assigned it to Eric Mark Golnik with no citation. QI concludes the adage is anonymous in the earliest citations, that there is evidence Tommy Hitchcock Sr. used it and his son relayed it, and that Whitney, Arnaz, Russell and others relayed but did not formulate it.

The saying "lose as if you like it" / "win as if you were used to it" appears nowhere on Wikiquote's Ralph Waldo Emerson page, in any section — not in the work-by-work sourced quotations, nor in the Attributed, Disputed or Misattributed sections (all of which are present on the page).
Ralph Waldo Emerson was born 25 May 1803 in Boston and died 27 April 1882 in Concord, Massachusetts; he worked as an essayist, lecturer, philosopher, minister and poet.

Tommy Hitchcock Jr. lived 11 February 1900 – 18 April 1944, carried a 10-goal polo handicap from 1922 to 1940, and was killed in a P-51 Mustang test crash near Salisbury, Wiltshire, England; his father was a U.S. Racing Hall of Fame horse trainer and 10-goal polo player who helped found the Meadow Brook Polo Club.

Thomas Hitchcock Sr. lived 23 November 1860 – 29 September 1941, organised the first polo match on Long Island in 1877, helped establish the Meadowbrook Polo Club in 1881, was one of the earliest American 10-goal players, is called the father of American steeplechase horse racing, won the American Grand National with Good and Plenty in 1906, and was inducted into the National Museum of Racing and Hall of Fame in 1973.
